title.value: Outcrop to Reservoir: Importance of Faulting to Hydrocarbon Migration in the Monterey Formation, CA

note.value:
Faulting is important for hydrocarbon migration in the siliceous shale units of the Monterey Formation. Field studies in the southern San Joaquin Valley and observations of other Monterey exposures throughout California show that both faulting and faults control hydrocarbon migration and accumulation. Shearing along pre-existing discontinuities, such as bedding planes or fractures, locally increases the permeability in the zone of deformation. As the rock is subjected to shear and begins to systematically fragment and subsequently brecciate, voids are created for hydrocarbon migration.

Hydrocarbon-filled breccia zones are exposed in the Antelope Shale at Chico Martinez Creek on the northeastern flank of the Temblor Range near McKittrick, California. Breccia zones occur parallel to bedding in porcelanite units (4 - 10 cm) and are bound above and below by siliceous shale beds (2 20 cm). Spacing between zones is a function of lithology and diagenesis. Alternating layers of pure and detrital rich layers of diatomaceous sediment were deposited, and the original composition subsequently influenced post-diagenetic material properties. Detrital-rich diatomite diagenetically alters to an incompetent siliceous shale (opal CT) while the cleaner sediments alter to a more brittle porcelanite (opal CT). Secondary fractures localize in the more brittle porcelanite in response to shearing along both bed parallel lithologic discontinuities and bed parallel fractures , and subsequently evolve into brecciated fault zones. In the Chico Martinez Creek outcrop, individual breccia zones combine to make an approximately 10 m package of hydrocarbon-filled breccia in which the individual zones are partially obliterated by deformation.

This conceptual model for hydrocarbon migration through the Monterey Formation, is applied to the subsurface. Using Formation Microscannerdata (FMS), we identify bed parallel breccia zones in the Antelope Shale at BuenaVista Hills (BVH) field. In the borehole image the brecciated-fault zone appears as unorganized patches of high and low resistivities with hints of bedding. At least one breccia zone identified in the borehole image can be directly correlated to hydrocarbon production determined by spinner flowmeter data. Although breccia zones are typically not recovered in core, there appears to be an association between fractures related to shearing processes and hydrocarbon transport. Oil-stained brecciated fracture zones, apparently associated with slip, occur both in Buena Vista Hills and other nearby fields producing from the AntelopeShale.

Dholakia, Sneha K. (1996). Outcrop to Reservoir: Importance of Faulting to Hydrocarbon Migration in the Monterey Formation, CA. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/qm319xj2346
